paper_title: Squoosh Bench: Evaluating UX-1 on 318 Historical Website A/B Tests

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Experimentation teams must decide which proposed website changes to test with live traffic. We evaluated whether forecasts from simulated shoppers could inform that choice. We screened 412 historical website A/B tests and evaluated four systems on the 318 that ran longer than 21 days. Each system predicted an original win, a variant win, or an inconclusive result. Page roles were masked and recorded outcomes were withheld during inference. Squoosh UX-1, a model fine-tuned on human browsing data, simulated 1,000 shoppers per arm and correctly classified 267 of 318 outcomes (84.0%, 95% Wilson interval 79.5-87.6%, treating experiments as independent). Qwen3 Next 80B, the strongest general-purpose configuration on outcome accuracy, correctly classified 196 of 318 (61.6%). UX-1 favored the variant in 126 experiments. In the live tests, 118 of those variants won (93.7%), four lost, and four had inconclusive results. The remaining 192 experiments included 19 additional variant wins.

sections.title: Practical implications for experimentation teams
sections.content: If team had tested the variants UX-1 favored first, its shortlist would have contained 126 of 318 candidates (39.6%) and 118 of the 137 variants that won their live tests (86.1%). Of the 126 variants UX-1 favored, 118 won their live tests (93.7%). The other 19 winners illustrate the cost of dropping candidate solely on its forecast.

sections.title: 1 Overview
sections.content: A team choosing its next live test has two reasons to care about forecast errors. Testing weak variant uses traffic that could go to another idea. Setting aside promising variant can leave real improvement undiscovered. We evaluated both decisions against the recorded outcomes of completed A/B tests. We screened 412 historical experiments and excluded 94 that ran for 21 days or fewer. Of the 318 experiments eligible for scoring, 113 favored the original page, 137 favored the variant, and 68 were inconclusive. UX-1 correctly classified 267 of the 318 outcomes (83.96% accuracy, 83.40% three-class balanced It correctly identified 94 original-page wins, 118 variant wins, and 55 inconclusive accuracy). outcomes. The most frequent outcome was variant win. rule that chose the variant in every experiment would therefore have classified 137 of 318 outcomes correctly (43.1%). This provides simple baseline for interpreting three-class accuracy. Among the 126 experiments where UX-1 favored the variant, 118 recorded variant win (93.7%). The frequency of variant wins in teams own test queue will affect how often its positive forecasts are correct. Benomar et al. (2026) evaluated persona-conditioned agents on 40 A/B tests and reported directional accuracy of 7590%, depending on the metric. Earlier Squoosh work examined when screenshot-based judge could abstain from choosing winner (Dooskin and Squoosh Technical Staff, 2026). An execution that produced no valid forecast was counted as failure. sections.title: 2.1 Eligibility and recorded outcomes
sections.content: Count 412 94 318 113 137 68 250 Experiments were eligible if their observed duration exceeded 21 days. We fixed the threshold before model scoring (SQ-DURATION-2026-08) and applied it before inspecting predictions. The 94 duration exclusions were outside the scoring denominator. 2 Duration was an eligibility criterion for this benchmark. The precision of human experiment also depends on sample size and how observations are correlated over time (Li and Yu, 2024). We selected 412 private partner A/B tests from larger collection and retained 318 after duration screening. Of the 412 screened, 97 had appeared in Squoosh AIs earlier report, Introducing Squoosh Bench. Partner agreements restrict disclosure of test sources. We withheld recorded outcomes during inference. The extent of site overlap with the models training data is unknown. For each eligible experiment, we assigned the recorded outcome using the prespecified primary conversion metric and the two-sided 95% confidence interval for the variant-minus-original effect. We classified the experiment as variant win when the interval lay entirely above zero, an originalpage win when it lay entirely below zero, and inconclusive when it included zero. We withheld the recorded outcome from all evaluated systems during inference.

sections.title: 3.1 UX-1 shopper model
sections.content: Squoosh UX-1 is the model that controls the simulated shoppers. We fine-tuned an open-source base model on dataset acquired by Squoosh that records how people interact with websites. The training goal was to capture variation in browsing decisions, such as whether shopper scrolls through listing, opens product page, or leaves before converting. For each page comparison, UX-1 simulated 1,000 shoppers on the original and 1,000 on the variant (2,000 shopper sessions in total). Both arms used the same device settings and primary conversion objective. UX-1 returned one categorical forecast for the comparison, signed relative-lift estimate, and brief explanation.

The resulting differences measure performance of the complete systems. This design does not isolate the effect of fine-tuning.

sections.content: We used anonymous page handles and removed identifying metadata to conceal page roles and recorded outcomes. The scorer restored the original and variant identities after predictions were locked. 4 Each system received the same pre-experiment information: planned exposure and allocation, the analysis rule, and available historical baseline information. We withheld observed treatment effects, conversion counts, and outcome statistics during inference. forecast received credit only when its locked call matched the recorded human outcome after the scorer restored the page identities. An inconclusive forecast therefore received credit only for an experiment whose recorded interval included zero. sections.title: 3.4 Runs and scoring
sections.content: We evaluated four systems on 318 eligible experiments. Each comparison included both pages. We held the random seed fixed within each UX-1 page comparison. Each system evaluated both presentation orders three times per experiment, with independent execution state for each repetition, yielding 7,632 executions. The primary analysis used the first repetition in the prespecified primary order for each system and experiment. Missing or invalid predictions received no credit and remained in the denominator. Outcome accuracy is the proportion of all 318 eligible experiments classified correctly. Three-class balanced accuracy is the unweighted mean of recall on original wins, variant wins, and inconclusive outcomes. For UX-1, the calculation was 1 3 (cid:18) 94 113 + 118 137 + (cid:19) 55 68 = 83.40% (UX-1). Winner-only accuracy is evaluated separately on the 250 directional outcomes. An inconclusive model prediction on one of these experiments receives no winner credit. To measure sensitivity to presentation order, we reversed the page order and mapped both predictions back to the original page identities. Two matching inconclusive calls counted as agreement.

sections.content: UX-1 matched 267 of 318 recorded outcomes (84.0%). Qwen3 Next 80B, the strongest generalpurpose configuration on outcome accuracy, matched 196 of 318 (61.64%). sections.title: 4.2 Inconclusive predictions and error structure
sections.content: Table 6: UX-1 outcome confusion matrix Recorded outcome Predicted original Predicted variant Predicted inconclusive Total Original wins Variant wins Inconclusive Total predictions 94 6 9 109 4 118 4 126 15 13 55 83 113 137 68 318 UX-1 recognizes 55 of the 68 recorded inconclusive outcomes, giving 80.88% inconclusive recall. UX-1 returned 83 inconclusive predictions. Fifty-five matched the recorded outcome (66.27% precision). The other 28 came from experiments with recorded winner. The 51 incorrect classifications comprise 10 wrong-direction predictions, 28 inconclusive predictions on directional outcomes, and 13 directional predictions on inconclusive outcomes. In one experiment involving popup, UX-1 predicted that the variant would outperform the original page on the primary conversion metric. The live A/B test favored the original page. This was one of four experiments in which UX-1 favored variant that went on to lose. UX-1 selected winner in 235 of 318 experiments (73.9% coverage). In 212 of those 235 cases (90.2%), the selected winner matched the human result. The other 23 comprised 10 opposite winners and 13 inconclusive human results.

sections.title: 4.3 Statistical uncertainty
sections.content: The Wilson 95% interval for outcome accuracy was 79.5387.59% (267/318). The corresponding intervals for class recall were 75.2388.96% for original wins, 79.3590.94% for variant wins, and 69.9988.47% for inconclusive results (Wilson, 1927). The eligible experiments spanned more than 40 sites. We calculated Wilson intervals using the experiment as the unit of analysis and assuming independence across experiments. Tests from the same site can share audiences and design features. If their prediction errors were positively correlated, the reported intervals may be too narrow (Hong et al., 2026). Changing one incorrect prediction to correct prediction increases overall accuracy by 0.31 percentage points and three-class balanced accuracy by 0.240.49 percentage points, depending on the recorded class.

sections.title: 4.5 Presentation-order consistency
sections.content: UX-1 returns the same mapped outcome in both presentation orders for 301/318 experiments, or 94.65%. Agreement after reversing page order included pairs of matching inconclusive calls. We used this metric to measure sensitivity to presentation order.

sections.title: 5 Interpretation for test prioritization
sections.content: UX-1 favored the variant in 126 of 318 experiments (39.6%). This group contained 118 of the 137 recorded variant wins (86.1%). Of the eight remaining experiments in the group, four favored the original on the primary metric and four were inconclusive. Outside that group, 19 variants won their live tests. Six came from the 109 experiments where UX-1 favored the original. Thirteen came from the 83 experiments where UX-1 predicted an inconclusive outcome. For team prioritizing live tests, those 13 cases illustrate the risk of dropping candidate solely because its forecast was inconclusive. These figures describe experiments that ran longer than 21 days. The duration criterion excluded shorter tests, which can include changes that show benefits or harms quickly as well as experiments that receive little traffic. The target was the conclusion of the historical experiment on its primary metric. For an effect close to the decision threshold, additional human exposure could change that conclusion. correct inconclusive forecast means the recorded test left the direction of the effect unresolved. The comparison estimates how the four systems performed with the page evidence, adapters, and resource budgets used here. Table 2 gives the industry mix of the evaluated experiments. The reported scores reflect the combined input of page evidence and permitted pre-experiment design information. For an experimentation team, these results support using forecast to decide which variants to test first. To evaluate that use on its own site, team could record forecasts before sending live traffic and test candidates both inside and outside the shortlist. That design would show how often the shortlisted variants win and how many winners the team would otherwise overlook.

We reran the benchmark and regenerated the result tables. The reported counts and scores were unchanged. Tables 1 and 2 describe the screening and composition of the corpus. Tables 47 report classification performance, presentation-order consistency, and lift error. Relative lift requires nonzero original conversion rate. Zero-denominator cases require separate absolute-effect treatment or exclusion from relative-lift scoring only. relative lift of 100% is valid when the original rate is positive. Reversing page order requires restoring the original denominator; simply negating relative percentage is insufficient. Of the 412 historical experiments screened, 318 met the duration criterion. UX-1 matched the recorded conclusion in 267 of those experiments, including 55 of the 68 with an inconclusive outcome.
